title: Interview: Sam Rivera — Senior Frontend Engineer

chapters.title: Intros and interview format
chapters.gist: Maya and Priya introduce themselves, Sam joins from Lisbon at 9 p.m. local time, and Maya lays out the 45-minute agenda.

chapters.title: Sam's background: fintech, offline-first app, TypeScript migration
chapters.gist: Sam describes five years at fintech Pagora, tech-leading an offline-first React Native app for field agents and a 14-month JavaScript-to-TypeScript migration across 300k lines that cut type-related incidents from about a quarter to under 10%.

chapters.title: Deep dive: offline sync, conflicts and idempotency
chapters.gist: Sam walks through a transactional outbox on SQLite, corrects themself that idempotency keys are generated on the client, explains moving from whole-record last-write-wins to per-field merges and intent-based money operations, and covers a queue that survives app kills with dead-lettering.

chapters.title: Working with design: pushing back with data
chapters.gist: Priya probes design collaboration; Sam tells how support-ticket data (30% of agent tickets were 'did it go through') led to a compromise sync indicator that cut those tickets about 40%, and how a designer rightly won an accessibility argument.

chapters.title: Design problem: proof of delivery with flaky connectivity
chapters.gist: Sam designs a driver proof-of-delivery flow that decouples a tiny 'delivered' event (with a ~20 KB thumbnail) from a resumable photo upload queue, adds glove-friendly capture, and openly flags limited maps and geospatial experience.

chapters.title: Sam's questions and interviewer debrief
chapters.gist: Sam asks about on-call, team size, product decisions and remote work, proposing a 1–9 p.m. Lisbon day for about 4 hours of Pacific overlap; after Sam leaves, Maya and Priya flag geospatial depth and the overlap as concerns and agree to advance Sam to the final round with Asher.

turns.t: Hey, Sam? Can you hear me okay?
Yeah, I can hear you. Hi. Hopefully the video's okay, my connection's been a little weird today, my neighbor is, I think, renovating the entire building.
No, you look great. Well, you look fine, I mean the video looks great. Priya should be jumping on any second, she was coming out of another call that I think ran over.
No worries at all.
So you're in Lisbon, right? What time is it there right now?
It's nine p.m. So, you know, I've had dinner, I've had a coffee, which was probably a mistake, but I'm wide awake. Very awake.
Sorry about that, we tried to find something earlier in your day and it just, the calendar did not cooperate this week.
Honestly it's fine. It's actually kind of a useful data point for both of us, right? Like, this is what the overlap actually looks like in practice.
Hi, sorry, sorry. Hi Sam, I'm Priya.
Hi Priya, nice to meet you.

Perfect timing. Okay so let me just do the quick framing and then we'll get into it. I'm Maya, I'm the engineering manager for the routing team at Tandem, which, despite the name, ends up owning a lot of stuff, including the driver app and the dispatcher dashboard on the frontend side. Priya leads design, so she works across all of that, and she's the person you'd be working with most closely on the design side. Today's about forty-five minutes. I'd like to spend the first chunk on your background, then go pretty deep on one technical area, I'm guessing offline sync because it's kind of all over your resume. Priya's going to ask about how you work with design. Then we'll do a small design problem, nothing with a whiteboard, no coding, just talking it through like we would on a real team. And then I want to save ten minutes or so for your questions, which, honestly, is the part I care about too. Sound good?
Sounds great, yeah.
And just so you know, we're recording this with Sounding, so we can take fewer notes and actually pay attention to you. Hannah mentioned that, I think?
Yeah, she did, that's totally fine.
Cool. So, give us the short version. Who are you, how'd you end up where you are.

Okay, short version. I'm Sam, I'm a frontend engineer, mostly React and React Native for the last, I guess, seven years total. I grew up outside Porto, studied computer science there, did a couple of years at an agency building, you know, marketing sites and the occasional e-commerce thing, which taught me a lot about shipping fast and very little about maintaining anything. And then I joined a fintech called Pagora, which is where I've been for the last five years. Pagora does small business lending, and a big part of the business is field agents, so people who go out and sign up small merchants, like shops, market stalls, that kind of thing, and then go back and collect repayments. A lot of them are in rural Portugal and in Mozambique, where the connectivity is, let's say, aspirational. So I ended up becoming kind of the offline person, which I didn't plan, but here we are.
Aspirational, I like that. So that app, the field agent app, that was React Native from the start?

It was React Native from the start but it was not offline-first from the start, which is kind of the whole story. When I joined it was a pretty standard app, you know, every screen fetched from the API, and if you didn't have a connection you got a spinner and then an error toast. And the agents just, they worked around it. They'd write things on paper and then type them in at night when they got back to wifi at a café or wherever. Which meant the data was a day late, and half the time there were typos, and the credit team hated it. So about a year in, me and one other engineer pitched rebuilding the data layer so the app worked offline by default. Local database on the device, every write goes to the local store first, and then there's a sync engine that pushes and pulls in the background. It took, honestly, longer than we said. We said four months, it was more like seven. But by the end, agents could do a full day with no signal and sync when they got back, and the paper went away, which was the real metric. The paper going away.
How big was the team on that?

On the mobile side we were three, at the peak four. Plus one backend engineer who was more or less dedicated to the sync endpoints, which was important. I don't think you can do this well if the sync protocol is designed only from one side. Like, if the backend just gives you REST endpoints and says good luck, you end up building a really fragile thing on the client.
Yeah. Agreed. And you were, were you leading that, or —

I was the tech lead on it, yeah. Not a manager, I've never managed people, but I wrote the design doc and I made most of the calls on the sync model, and I made some bad ones, which we'll probably get to. I also did a lot of the unglamorous stuff, like the rollout. We had about four hundred agents with the old app, some of them with unsent drafts sitting on their phones, so we couldn't just flip a switch. We shipped it behind a flag, region by region, starting with the agents closest to the office so we could literally drive over if something broke.
We will definitely get to those. Before we do, the TypeScript thing. Three hundred thousand lines is a lot of lines. Tell me about that.

Yeah, so, that was a different kind of project. Less fun, honestly more impactful. So by year three we had, across the mobile app and the agent web portal and a shared package, about three hundred thousand lines of JavaScript. Some Flow annotations in places, which, you know, Flow. And we were having a lot of bugs that were just shape bugs. Something's undefined, something's a string instead of a number, the API changed a field name and nobody noticed for a week. So I pushed for moving to TypeScript and ended up leading it. The way we did it, we didn't do a big bang. We turned on allowJs, so JS and TS could live together, we added a lint rule that said no new JS files, period, and then we migrated bottom-up. Shared utilities and the API client first, because everything depends on those, so typing them gave you the most value per line. Then the data layer, then screens. We used Airbnb's ts-migrate for the first pass on some of the bigger directories, which gets you to compiling but with a lot of any. And then we had a little dashboard that tracked percent of files converted and the count of explicit anys, and we posted it in the channel every Friday. Kind of silly, but people liked watching the number go down.
The Friday number, I love that.
It worked weirdly well. People would sneak in an extra file on Thursday afternoon so their team looked good.
How long did it take, end to end?

About fourteen months to get to fully TypeScript, and then strict mode was another, I want to say, three months after that. We did strict per directory, with a tsconfig that extended the base one, so the newer code was strict before the old stuff was. Which meant for a while you had two sets of rules depending on which folder you were in, which people complained about, but it let us move without stopping feature work.
And did it actually move the bug numbers? Or was it more of a, you know, developer happiness thing.

Both, but I can give you a real number. We tagged production incidents by root cause, and the type-related category, so undefined access, wrong shape, that kind of thing, went from roughly a quarter of our mobile incidents to under ten percent. I don't want to oversell that, part of it was also that we added contract tests on the API at the same time. So it's not all TypeScript. But it was a big part of it.
That's a really honest answer, thank you. Most people just tell me it cut bugs by eighty percent.
I mean, I could say that. I'd be lying, but I could say it.

Okay so let's go into the sync engine, because this is pretty close to stuff we deal with every day. Our drivers lose signal constantly, loading docks, parking garages, rural routes. Walk me through the architecture. Like, what's on the device, what happens when an agent hits save.

Sure. So on device we had SQLite, through WatermelonDB at first and later we moved to a thinner layer on top of op-sqlite because Watermelon's sync assumptions didn't fit us perfectly. When an agent does anything, say they record a repayment or they update a merchant's phone number, two things happen in one transaction. The local record gets updated, so the UI reflects it immediately, and we append an operation to an outbox table. The operation is like, type, entity id, the payload, a created-at, and an idempotency key. And the transaction matters, because if you update the record and then crash before writing the outbox entry, you've got a change that looks saved but never syncs. So it's both or neither.
Mm-hm.

Then there's a sync worker that drains the outbox. It sends operations in order per entity. It doesn't have to be globally ordered, but for a given merchant you want them in order, otherwise you get an update arriving before the create and the server's confused. When the server acks an operation, we mark it done and eventually delete it. And on the pull side, we kept a cursor, basically a server-side change sequence number, and the device asks for everything since its last cursor.
And the idempotency key, where does that come from?

So the server generates it when it first sees the request, and then — no, wait, sorry, that's backwards. That's completely backwards. The client generates it, at the moment the operation goes into the outbox. A UUID, v4 originally, later we used v7 because they sort by time, which was nice for debugging. It has to be the client, because the whole point is the case where the request reaches the server, the server applies it, and then the response gets lost because the agent walked into a basement. The client doesn't know if it worked, so it retries, and the retry has to carry the same key so the server can say, oh, I've seen this one, here's the original result. If the server generated the key, the retry would just look like a brand new request. Sorry, it's nine p.m., I'm going to blame the coffee.
No, that's good, you caught it. And how long does the server remember keys?

We kept them for seventy-two hours in a table keyed on device id plus the key. Which was based on, we looked at the longest realistic offline stretch, and agents in the field could go two days without signal, so seventy-two gave us a bit of margin. Beyond that, the operation itself had enough information that most things were naturally idempotent anyway, but not all of them.
Okay. Conflicts. Two agents edit the same merchant offline. What happens?

Yeah, so this is the bad call I mentioned. The first version was last write wins on the whole record. Each record had an updated-at, the later one wins, done. It's simple and it's easy to explain and it's wrong for us. Because what happened in practice is one agent updates the merchant's phone number in the morning, another agent, a different one, visits in the afternoon and updates the address, they both sync that night, and whoever syncs last overwrites the entire record. So you lose the phone number. And nobody notices until a collections call goes to the old number. We had, I think, a few hundred of those before we really understood the pattern.
Ouch.

Yeah. And also the timestamps were device clocks, so even 'later' was kind of a lie. One agent had their phone set to the wrong year. Literally the wrong year. So their writes won everything for about a week.
Oh no.

So we moved to per-field merges. Each field carries its own version, and the operation only sends the fields that actually changed, not the whole record. So phone and address don't conflict at all anymore, they're different fields, both changes survive. And for ordering we stopped trusting device clocks for conflict decisions, we used the server's sequence, so the version the client last saw. If you edit a field and the server's version of that field has moved since you last pulled, that's a real conflict, and then you need a policy.
And what was the policy?

Depends on the field, which is the honest answer. For most profile stuff, phone, address, opening hours, it's still last write wins but at the field level, by server arrival order, and we kept the losing value in a history table so support could recover it. For a few things we surfaced it to a human, like if two agents changed the merchant's legal name we flagged it for review instead of picking. And for money we just didn't do state merges at all.
Say more about that.

So the mistake you can make with money is syncing the balance. Like the client says, balance is now four hundred and fifty. If two agents both collect fifty euros offline from the same merchant, which did happen, family businesses, one cousin pays one agent and the other cousin pays the other, you end up with both clients saying balance is four-fifty and you've lost fifty euros. So instead the client never sends a balance. It sends an intent. Record payment of fifty euros, with the receipt number and the key. The server is the only thing that computes the balance, by applying the intents. Those commute, two payments of fifty is a hundred, order doesn't matter. The client shows a projected balance locally, with a little marker that says pending, but it's not authoritative.
Yeah. That's the right answer. We have the same split with stop status, kind of. Like 'mark delivered' is an event, not a field you overwrite.
Right, exactly. Events are so much easier to reason about than state when you're offline.

Okay, last piece, the queue surviving the app being killed. Because on Android especially, drivers swipe the app away, the OS kills it, the battery saver kills it. How did you make sure stuff actually got sent?

So the first principle is the outbox is on disk, in SQLite, so the app dying doesn't lose anything, it just delays it. Nothing is ever only in memory. The second part is getting it to actually flush. On Android we used WorkManager with a network-connected constraint, through a small native module, so when connectivity comes back the OS wakes us up even if the app's not running, and we run a headless JS task that drains the outbox. That was pretty reliable, except on some Xiaomi and Huawei phones with aggressive battery stuff, where we had to walk agents through whitelisting the app, which, not fun. On iOS it's worse, background fetch is basically whenever the OS feels like it, so we leaned on flushing whenever the app comes to the foreground, and on any network change while it's open. And we showed a count. Like 'three changes waiting to sync.' That turned out to matter a lot, actually, which is maybe a good segue for Priya.
Ha, hold that thought one sec. What about poison messages? Something the server rejects every single time.

Yeah, we had a retry policy with exponential backoff and jitter, and after a certain number of failures with a non-retryable error, like a validation error, a four-hundred class thing, we moved it to a dead-letter state. It stays on the device, it doesn't block the rest of the queue for other entities, and it shows up in a 'needs attention' list for the agent with a plain-language reason. The important thing was it didn't block other merchants' operations. Early on we had one bad operation that jammed the entire queue for an agent for two days. That's how we learned.
Everyone learns that one the hard way. How did you test any of this, by the way? Offline bugs are miserable to reproduce.

I think jamming the queue is mandatory, it's a rite of passage. Testing-wise, mostly by making the bad network reproducible on purpose. In dev builds we had a fake network layer with a little debug menu, so you could say drop every third request, or add four seconds of latency, or succeed on the server but lose the response, which is the nasty one. QA would run whole days in that mode. And on the server side we had a property-based test that took a random batch of operations, shuffled them, duplicated some, delivered them in different orders, and checked the final state always came out the same. That caught a lot of stuff we'd never have thought to write a test for. And honestly, a couple of us went out with agents once a quarter. Nothing replaces sitting in a car in the middle of nowhere with one bar, watching someone actually use the thing.
Okay, Priya, you've been very patient.

No, this was great, honestly. So, my turn. On our side the driver app and the dashboard are pretty design-heavy, and I work really closely with the frontend engineers, like we pair a lot. So I'm curious how you've worked with designers. And maybe specifically, tell me about a time you disagreed with a design. What happened?

Yeah, okay, I have a good one, and it's actually related to the sync count thing. So when we did the offline rebuild, our designer at the time, Inês, she's great, she had this really strong principle that the agent shouldn't have to think about sync. Which I agree with, as a goal. And so her designs didn't show sync status anywhere. Things just saved, and the idea was the app would handle it invisibly, which is, you know, the dream.
Sure, that's very much the instinct.

And my gut said that's not going to work for these users, because they've been burned. They've had the old app eat their data. But a gut feeling isn't an argument, so instead of saying 'I think you're wrong,' I went and pulled support tickets from the previous quarter and tagged them. And roughly thirty percent of all tickets from field agents were some version of 'did my submission go through.' Not 'it failed,' just 'I don't know if it worked.' And then we had a handful of session recordings, with consent, where you could see agents submitting the same repayment two or three times because there was no feedback. Which, side note, is part of why idempotency mattered so much.
Right, right.

So I brought that to Inês, and I didn't bring a design, I just brought the data and said, here's the problem I think we're going to create. And she pushed back on some of it, which was fair, she said a big sync status bar would make agents anxious and they'd just stare at it all day. And she was right about that, actually. So we landed in the middle. A small indicator in the header, a little cloud icon with a number, that only shows up when there's something pending, and a sync history screen you can tap into if you care. And per item, like a little clock on a repayment that hasn't synced yet, which turns into a check.
And did it work? Did you measure it?

We did a quick test with five agents first, just in person at the office in Coimbra, before we built the full thing. And then after launch the 'did it go through' tickets dropped by, it was about forty percent over the next two months. Not to zero. Some people will always call. But the duplicate submissions mostly stopped.
That's a really nice story. I like that you brought the problem and not a solution.
I learned that the hard way too, honestly. Early in my career I'd show up with a Figma file I made myself and say, 'what about this,' and designers, quite reasonably, hated that.
Yeah, we do. A little.
Fair.
What about the other direction? Like when design pushed you on something you didn't want to do.

Oh, all the time. The one that comes to mind is accessibility. Inês pushed really hard for proper dynamic type support, because a lot of our agents were older and turned the font size way up on their phones. And I resisted, because our layouts were built with fixed heights everywhere and it was going to be a lot of work. And she just, she went and borrowed a phone from one of the agents with the font cranked all the way up, and showed me the app, and half the buttons were cut off. So, yeah. She won that one, rightly. That took us like three sprints.
That's the best way to win that argument.
It was very effective. I couldn't argue with the phone.
Last one from me, how do you like to work day to day with a designer? Like, when do you want to get pulled in?

Early, but not to make decisions. I like being in the room when the problem's being framed, mostly so I can say early, 'hey, this part's going to be expensive' or 'this part's basically free, we already have it.' Because designers don't always know what's cheap. And then I like a lot of small check-ins while building, rather than a big handoff and a big review. Like, I'll send a screen recording from a branch, 'here's how this transition feels on a real device,' because stuff that looks good in Figma can feel terrible on a five-year-old Android phone. Which is what most field workers have.
God, yes. Our drivers too. We test on a, I think it's a Galaxy A12, that's the baseline.
Exactly. That's the real target device.

Okay, let's do the design problem, we've got about, yeah, twenty minutes left, so let's give this ten or twelve. So here's the setup. You're building the delivery flow in a driver app. Driver pulls up to a stop, delivers the package, and has to capture proof of delivery, which is one or more photos, sometimes a signature. Connectivity is flaky, like, could be fine, could be nothing for an hour in a rural stretch, could be one bar in a loading dock. Dispatch wants to know as soon as possible that the stop is done. And the customer, the shipper, wants the photo, because that's how they resolve 'I never got my package' disputes. How would you approach it?
Okay. Can I ask a couple of questions first?
Please.
How many photos per stop, typically, and are they, like, required? Can a driver complete a stop without one?
Usually one, sometimes two or three for freight. Required for most customers. Some shippers make it optional.
And how many stops in a day? Ballpark.
Parcel and grocery, call it eighty to a hundred and fifty. Freight a lot fewer, maybe ten or fifteen, but bigger.
Okay, and last one, how long does the photo need to be kept on the device? Like is there a legal thing, or is it just until it's uploaded?
Let's say just until it's safely on the server.

Cool. So, I'd split it into three things that are actually pretty different. There's capture, there's the stop completion as an event, and there's the photo upload. And the main design decision is that those are decoupled. The driver should never be waiting on the network to move to the next stop.
Okay.

So capture first. Driver hits 'complete,' camera opens, they take the photo. The moment they accept it, we write it to app storage, not the camera roll, the app's own directory, and we compute a hash. We also capture metadata, the stop id, the GPS fix and its accuracy, the timestamp, both wall clock and a monotonic one in case the device clock is wrong, which, as we established, it will be. Then we compress on device. A full camera photo is like four or five megabytes, and for proof of delivery you need, what, long edge sixteen hundred pixels, JPEG at decent quality, you're around two to three hundred kilobytes. That's ten to twenty times less to upload over a bad connection, which is probably the biggest single win in this whole thing.
Do you keep the original?

I'd say no, unless the shipper needs it for some legal reason. Keeping originals is how you fill up a driver's phone by Wednesday. Which leads to the other thing, I'd check free storage at the start of the shift and warn if it's low, because you don't want to discover that at stop ninety.
That happens. That literally happens.

I believe it. Okay so then the completion. In the same local transaction as saving the photo, we write a 'stop delivered' event to the outbox. That event is tiny, it's like a few hundred bytes, it includes the photo hash and a reference, but not the photo itself. And I'd also generate a really small thumbnail, like twenty kilobytes, maybe less, and attach that to the event. So the moment there's any connection at all, even a terrible one, dispatch gets 'stop twelve delivered at 2:14, here's a tiny preview, full photo pending.' And the UI moves the driver on to the next stop immediately.
Why the thumbnail?

Two reasons. One, dispatch gets something to look at fast, which honestly covers most of the disputes, like, 'yes, it's on the porch.' And two, it's insurance. If the phone dies, or gets dropped in a canal, or the driver uninstalls the app before the full photo uploads, you at least have the thumbnail on the server. It's not great evidence, but it's a lot better than nothing.
Okay, I like that.

Then the photo upload is its own queue, separate from the event outbox, because you don't want a three hundred kilobyte upload stuck on bad signal blocking the small events behind it. That's the head-of-line thing again. I'd have the client request a presigned upload URL, and use a resumable upload, either chunked multipart or something like the tus protocol, so if you're at eighty percent and lose signal you don't start over. The server verifies the hash when it's done and then acks. And only after that ack do we delete the local file. Never before.
What about when they're on a cell connection that's technically up but awful? Like one bar.

Yeah, that's honestly a harder case than no connection. With no connection you just wait. With a bad one you can burn battery and data retrying forever. So I'd use small chunks, maybe two fifty-six kilobytes, timeouts that adapt to recent throughput, and backoff with jitter. And I'd prioritize: events first, always, then photos oldest first. And, if the shipper allows it, the depot wifi at end of shift is the backstop. So you'd show the dispatcher a stop as delivered, photo pending, and you'd expect the long tail to clear when they get back to the depot.
Can I ask about the driver side for a sec? Because the thing I think about is, the driver is holding a box, maybe wearing gloves, it's raining, there's glare. What does that screen look like to you?

Yeah, totally. So I'd want the capture to be basically one big button. The camera opens straight away when you hit complete, no extra screen in between. Big shutter button, reachable with a thumb, works with gloves, which means big targets, honestly bigger than feels right in Figma. A quick review, 'use this photo or retake,' and I'd lean on auto-accepting after a second or two unless they tap retake, because every extra tap at a hundred stops a day adds up. And the sync state should be visible but quiet. Like the stop in the list gets a little upload icon until the photo's on the server, and there's a count somewhere, 'two photos uploading.' Same lesson as before. Drivers will want to know their proof is safe, because if there's a dispute it's on them.
Yeah. That's a real thing, drivers get blamed.
Right, so it's not just a UX nicety, it's, like, their job security.

Okay, one more angle. Location. Say the shipper wants to verify the driver was actually at the address when they took the photo. And dispatch wants to see the stops on a map. How would you handle that part?

So, I'll be upfront, this is where my experience is thinner. I've done basic stuff, capturing GPS with accuracy, and I've done a simple geofence check, like is this point within some radius of the stop's coordinates, haversine distance, that kind of thing. I'd record the GPS fix and its accuracy with the photo, and I'd flag, not block, deliveries where the fix is more than, I don't know, a hundred and fifty meters from the address, because blocking is going to fail in exactly the places you don't want it to fail, like big apartment complexes or GPS bouncing around downtown between tall buildings. But the map side, rendering lots of stops, clustering, route lines, offline map tiles, I've only done that in a side project with Mapbox. I haven't done it at scale in production. I'd want to lean on whoever on the team has, and I'd learn it, but I don't want to pretend.
No, I appreciate that. It's good to know. And the flagging instead of blocking, that's the right instinct, we got burned on that exact thing.
The apartment complex thing?
The apartment complex thing. Okay, anything you'd want to add before we move on?

Just one, observability. I'd want metrics from the client on queue depth and time to upload, like p50 and p95 from capture to server ack, per region. Because otherwise you'll never know which areas are actually bad until a shipper complains.
Yep. Okay, great.
So, your turn. What do you want to know?
Okay, I have a list, I'll try to be quick. First, on-call. What does it look like for frontend engineers?

So frontend engineers are in a rotation, but it's a separate, lighter rotation from the backend one. It's mostly the dashboard and the driver app releases. Right now it's about one week in eight. And, being honest with you, we had an outage last Thursday, the ETA service was down for about forty-seven minutes, and that was a backend issue, a Redis failover that turned into a retry storm. The frontend on-call wasn't paged into the fix, but they were in the incident channel helping with customer comms. We're also, we're working on getting the status page updated faster, that was not our best moment.
That's fair, thanks for telling me. And would on-call be in my hours, or —

We'd set it up so your on-call hours are your working hours, with a backup on Pacific time. We're not going to page you at three a.m. Lisbon time for a dashboard bug. I'll send you the on-call doc after this, it's short, it'll answer the rest.
Okay, good. Second, team size. How many people would I actually be working with?

So my org is eleven engineers right now, across routing, the ML side with Kenji, platform with Ravi, and the apps. We're hiring two senior frontend engineers, and they'd mostly sit on the driver app and the dispatcher dashboard. Day to day you'd be working with probably four or five people, plus Priya, plus Daniel, he's our staff engineer, he's kind of everywhere.
Got it. And how do product decisions get made? Like, who decides what gets built, and how much does engineering get a say?

Our head of product is Asher, you'll probably meet him in the next round. The way it works, roughly, is the quarterly priorities get set in planning, product, design, eng, sales is in there too. And within that, teams have a lot of room. Engineers write the design docs, they're in customer calls sometimes. I'll be honest, it's a sixty-person startup, so sometimes things come in sideways, a big customer wants something, a deal needs something. That's part of the job. I think engineering has a real voice, but you have to use it.
And design is pretty embedded. Like, an engineer on the driver app would be in the onboarding research sessions with me, we're redoing that whole flow right now.

That sounds great, actually. Okay, last one, and it's kind of the big one for me. Remote, and specifically time zones. I'm in Lisbon, I'm not planning to move. Most of the team is Pacific, right? What's the overlap you'd expect?

Yeah, most of us are Pacific, a few people in Seattle and one in Toronto. We're remote-first, there's no office requirement, but most of the team works roughly nine to five Pacific. What were you thinking for your hours?

So I've thought about this. I'd shift my day, work something like one p.m. to nine p.m. Lisbon. That's, right now, nine a.m. to one p.m. Pacific, so about four hours of overlap. And honestly I'm a bit of a night owl anyway, so it's not a sacrifice. And my mornings would be focus time, which you'd kind of get for free since everyone's asleep.

Four hours is workable. I won't pretend it's the same as being here. Planning would land in your evening, and there'll be days where something blows up at three p.m. Pacific and you're offline. So we'd want to be deliberate about async, like, writing things down, doing handoff notes at the end of your day, recording design reviews so you can watch them in the morning. Which honestly we should be doing anyway, so in a way it'd be good for us.
That's fair. I'd rather hear that than 'oh, time zones are no problem.'
Ha. Yeah. Anything else?
No, I think that's it. Thank you both, this was genuinely fun. The proof-of-delivery thing, I'm going to be thinking about that for a while.
Thanks Sam, really nice to meet you.
Thanks Sam. Hannah will be in touch about next steps, probably in the next couple of days. Enjoy the rest of your evening. Go to bed.
I'll try. Bye!
Okay, Sam's off. Quick gut check while it's fresh?

Strong. Like, really strong. The design story was one of the best answers I've heard to that question. Brought data, didn't bring a solution, and then admitted the designer was right about the anxiety thing. That's exactly what I want. And on the delivery flow, the gloves and glare stuff, they got there without me having to drag it out of them.

Yeah, I'm in the same place. Technically it's the strongest frontend candidate we've talked to. The sync stuff was real, like, you can't make up the wrong-year phone story. Intents instead of balances, the thumbnail as insurance, decoupling the event from the upload, that's all exactly how I'd want someone on the driver app to think. And the idempotency slip, honestly, catching it themselves was a plus, not a minus.
Totally. Concerns?

Two. Maps and geospatial. They were upfront about it, but it's thin, and a lot of the dashboard work is map-heavy, clustering, live positions, all of that. I think it's learnable, and Daniel can pair, but it's a real gap. And the time zone. Four hours of overlap is workable, but it's on the low end, and it's going to cost us something during weeks like last week.
Yeah, the time zone one is the one I'd watch. For the onboarding work we do a lot of live jam sessions. But four hours is enough if we plan for it.

Okay, so I think the recommendation is advance to the final round with Asher. I'll write that up. And I'll ask Asher to dig into the maps gap and the overlap specifically, so we're not just hand-waving it. Like, for the maps thing, maybe he walks them through the dispatcher map and asks how they'd approach clustering a few thousand live vehicles, just to see how they reason about something they haven't done. And for the overlap, a concrete scenario. It's three p.m. Pacific, the dashboard's broken for a big customer, Sam's been offline for two hours. What does the handoff look like.
Agreed. I'll get my scorecard in tonight.
Mine'll be in by tomorrow morning. I'll ping Hannah to get the final scheduled, ideally next week. We don't want to lose this one.
No, we really don't. Okay, bye.
Bye.

items.text: Senior Frontend Engineer technical interview (driver app and dispatcher dashboard): background, an offline-sync deep dive, design collaboration with Priya, a proof-of-delivery design problem, and Sam's questions.

Sam spent 5 years at fintech Pagora as tech lead of an offline-first React Native app for field agents in rural Portugal and Mozambique; the rebuild took 7 months against a 4-month estimate and eliminated paper workarounds.
Sync knowledge is deep and earned in production: moved from whole-record last-write-wins to per-field merges after losing data, and syncs money as commutative intents rather than balances.
Sam briefly said the server generates idempotency keys, then corrected it unprompted: keys are client-generated at enqueue time so retries after a lost response dedupe.
Best-in-loop design collaboration answer: brought support-ticket data (30% of agent tickets were 'did it go through') instead of a mockup, and conceded the designer's point about anxiety.
Concerns: maps/geospatial experience is limited to a Mapbox side project, and Sam's proposed 1–9 p.m. Lisbon day gives about 4 hours of Pacific overlap.
Recommendation: advance to the final round with Asher.
About 7 years in React/React Native: agency work, then 5 years at Pagora (small-business lending with field agents).
Led a bottom-up JS-to-TypeScript migration of ~300k lines using allowJs, a no-new-JS lint rule, ts-migrate, and a Friday progress dashboard.
Took ~14 months to full TypeScript plus ~3 months to strict mode, enabled per directory.
Type-related incidents fell from about a quarter of mobile incidents to under 10%; Sam credited API contract tests for part of it rather than overclaiming.
SQLite (WatermelonDB, later op-sqlite) with a transactional outbox: record update and outbox append commit together or not at all.
Server retains idempotency keys for 72 hours keyed on device id + key, sized to agents' longest realistic two-day offline stretch.
Per-field versions ordered by server sequence, not device clocks (one agent's phone was set to the wrong year); losing values kept in a history table.
Outbox lives on disk; Android flushes via WorkManager and a headless JS task, iOS flushes on foreground and network changes.
Non-retryable failures move to a dead-letter 'needs attention' list so one bad operation can't jam the queue.
Tested with a fault-injecting network layer in dev builds and server-side property tests that shuffle and duplicate operations.
Compromise with designer Inês: a small pending-sync indicator, a sync history screen, and per-item clock-to-check status.
Validated with 5 agents in Coimbra; 'did it go through' tickets dropped ~40% over two months and duplicate submissions mostly stopped.
Lost an argument over dynamic type to a phone with the font cranked up; took three sprints to fix.
Prefers joining problem framing early and frequent small check-ins with real-device recordings over big handoffs.
Decoupled capture, the 'delivered' event, and the photo upload so the driver never waits on the network.
Compress on device from 4–5 MB to roughly 200–300 KB and capture GPS accuracy plus wall-clock and monotonic timestamps.
A tiny delivered event with a ~20 KB thumbnail goes first, giving dispatch a fast preview and insurance if the phone dies.
Separate resumable upload queue (presigned URLs, chunked or tus); local file deleted only after a hash-verified server ack.
Glove-friendly one-button capture with auto-accept, plus quiet upload status so drivers know their proof is safe.
Would flag rather than block deliveries more than ~150 m from the address; candidly limited on maps rendering and clustering.
Frontend on-call is a lighter rotation, about one week in eight; Sam's on-call would match their working hours with a Pacific backup.
Sam stays in Lisbon and proposes working 1–9 p.m. local, about 9 a.m.–1 p.m. Pacific.
Maya was candid that planning would land in Sam's evening and the team would need stronger async habits.

ask.q: How did Sam handle sync conflicts at Pagora?
ask.a: The first version used whole-record last-write-wins, which lost data when two agents edited different fields of the same merchant, made worse by device clocks (one phone was set to the wrong year). Sam moved to per-field versions ordered by server sequence, kept losing values in a history table, and sent legal-name conflicts to human review. For money, the client sends commutative intents like 'record payment of €50' and only the server computes balances.

ask.q: What detail did Sam get wrong, and how did they correct it?
ask.a: Sam first said the server generates the idempotency key, then immediately corrected it: the client generates a UUID when the operation enters the outbox. That way a retry after a lost response carries the same key and the server can return the original result. Maya saw the self-correction as a plus.

ask.q: How would Sam design proof-of-delivery photos for drivers with flaky connectivity?
ask.a: Sam would decouple capture, the 'delivered' event and the photo upload. The photo is compressed on device to roughly 200–300 KB, and a tiny delivered event carrying a ~20 KB thumbnail goes out first so dispatch sees it fast and has insurance if the phone dies. Full photos go through a separate resumable upload queue and are deleted locally only after a hash-verified server ack.

ask.q: What are the concerns about Sam?
ask.a: Two. Maps and geospatial experience is thin (basic geofencing, plus Mapbox only in a side project), which matters because the dashboard is map-heavy, though Daniel could pair. And Sam would work 1–9 p.m. Lisbon, giving only about 4 hours of overlap with Pacific.

ask.q: What working hours did Sam propose, and how much overlap is that?
ask.a: Sam is staying in Lisbon and would work roughly 1–9 p.m. local time, which is about 9 a.m.–1 p.m. Pacific, or 4 hours of overlap. Maya called it workable but said planning would land in Sam's evening and the team would need better async habits, like handoff notes and recorded design reviews.

ask.q: What's the recommendation and next step for Sam?
ask.a: Maya and Priya both rated Sam the strongest frontend candidate so far and recommend advancing to the final round with Asher. Maya will ask Asher to probe map clustering and a concrete late-Pacific incident handoff. Priya submits her scorecard tonight, and Maya submits hers by morning and asks Hannah to schedule the final next week.
